q: Does Singapore's mandatory climate reporting apply to my Indian group's Singapore company?
title: Singapore climate reporting for Indian groups
short: Only if the Singapore company is listed on SGX or is a large non-listed company with annual revenue of at least SGD 1 billion and total assets of at least SGD 500 million. Most holding companies miss the revenue test. Listed issuers report from FY2025; the non-listed start was deferred in August 2025.
audience: Indian groups with Singapore holding or trading companies

sections.h: Test your Singapore company in three steps
ol: Is it listed on SGX? Then it is in the listed issuer regime, reporting climate disclosures based on the ISSB standards, starting with Scope 1 and Scope 2 from FY2025.

If not listed, does it have revenue of at least SGD 1 billion and total assets of at least SGD 500 million? It must pass both. A holding company with large assets but dividend income only usually fails the revenue test; a commodity or trading company may pass.
If it passes, check whether an exemption applies, such as a parent that already publishes group climate disclosures covering it under ISSB standards or an equivalent framework.

p: ACRA and SGX RegCo first set FY2027 as the start for large non-listed companies and phased in Scope 3 later for everyone. In August 2025 they deferred Scope 3 and the non-listed timeline. Read the current ACRA dates for your financial year before planning, as these were revised once already.

sections.h: Why your Indian plants may be in the report
p: If the Singapore company owns the Indian operating companies and prepares consolidated accounts, its disclosures cover the group it consolidates. Scope 1 and Scope 2 then include the fuel and electricity of Indian factories, measured by the GHG Protocol as the ISSB standard requires. A trading company that owns no plants reports its own offices and any assets it controls.

sections.h: How this differs from India's BRSR
p: BRSR is filed by the top 1,000 listed companies in India in SEBI's format. Singapore's regime uses the ISSB standards. An Indian parent's BRSR is not automatically an ISSB report, so do not assume it gives the Singapore company an exemption; check with your Singapore adviser.

senseible: Senseible turns the fuel invoices and electricity bills of Indian sites into document-backed Scope 1 and Scope 2 figures that a Singapore parent can consolidate. It does not decide whether ACRA or SGX rules apply or prepare ISSB statements.
